ai.definition: Quantum cryptography leverages principles of quantum mechanics, specifically the properties of qubits, to create unbreakable cryptographic keys that are used in secure communication protocols.
ai.howItWorks: Qubits, due to their superposition and entanglement properties, enable the creation of encryption keys that cannot be intercepted or tampered with without detection. This is achieved through quantum key distribution (QKD) methods such as BB84 or E91 schemes, where any attempt at eavesdropping will alter the qubits' state, thus alerting both communicating parties to potential security breaches.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the vulnerability of classical cryptography to quantum computing attacks and provides a method for secure key exchange that is theoretically unbreakable by quantum computers in the future.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating qubits using various techniques such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, or photonic systems. These qubits are then integrated into devices capable of performing QKD protocols.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing and fabricating quantum devices, integrating them with classical communication infrastructure, and testing for security and performance.
ai.costDrivers: High initial costs due to the complexity of creating and maintaining quantum systems. Additionally, the need for specialized cooling and shielding environments adds to operational expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected growth driven by increasing demand for secure communication in government, finance, and critical infrastructure sectors.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still being developed. Initial focus on national security and financial regulations with potential future expansion into broader cybersecurity policies.
ai.risks: Technological risks include the need for continuous innovation to keep pace with advancements in quantum computing. Operational risks involve maintaining secure environments and preventing physical attacks on quantum devices.
ai.profitability: Potential high profitability due to the unique value proposition of unbreakable encryption, but currently limited by high costs and narrow market penetration.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving qubit stability, increasing transmission distances, and reducing system costs. Integration with existing communication networks is also a key area for advancement.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and cooling requirements.

glossary.def: The basic unit of quantum information, analogous to a classical bit but capable of existing in multiple states simultaneously.
A method for securely distributing cryptographic keys using the principles of quantum mechanics to ensure that any eavesdropping will be detected.
The principle in quantum mechanics where a qubit can exist in multiple states simultaneously until measured.

A phenomenon in quantum physics where pairs or groups of particles interact in such a way that the state of one particle cannot be described independently of the state of the others, even when the particles are separated by large distances.

subsystems.name: Photon source
subsystems.role: emits single photons, or very weak laser pulses, each encoding one bit of the key.

subsystems.name: Quantum channel
subsystems.role: carries the photons; any attempt to read them disturbs them and leaves a trace.

subsystems.name: Detector station
subsystems.role: measures each arriving photon in a randomly chosen basis.

subsystems.name: Classical authenticated channel
subsystems.role: public but tamper-proof channel used to compare bases, estimate eavesdropping and confirm the key.

subsystems.name: Key management layer
subsystems.role: stores keys, decides when enough entropy exists, and feeds them to encrypting equipment.

subsystems.name: Relay or repeater
subsystems.role: extends reach beyond the range of a single link.

buildSteps.title: Choose the route
buildSteps.detail: Two sites are linked by dedicated fibre or a clear line of sight; losses are measured because every decibel cuts the key rate.

buildSteps.title: Send single photons
buildSteps.detail: A laser is attenuated or a source is engineered so that pulses contain on average far less than one photon, encoding bits in phase or polarisation.

buildSteps.title: Measure on the other side
buildSteps.detail: The receiver randomly picks a measurement basis for each photon, recording a click or no-click.

buildSteps.title: Sift the key
buildSteps.detail: Over the authenticated public channel the two sides reveal only which bases they used, keeping the bits where the bases matched.

buildSteps.title: Estimate eavesdropping
buildSteps.detail: They sample some bits to measure the error rate; above a threshold the key is thrown away.

buildSteps.title: Distil a secret key
buildSteps.detail: Error correction fixes remaining mismatches, then privacy amplification hashes the string so an eavesdropper's partial knowledge is squeezed out.

buildSteps.title: Authenticate and use
buildSteps.detail: The key is used with a one-time pad or to refresh a symmetric cipher such as AES — the quantum part distributes keys, it does not encrypt data itself.

buildSteps.title: Extend the network
buildSteps.detail: Trusted nodes or, in future, quantum repeaters chain links together into a metro or national network.

prerequisites.why: without counting individual photons there is no way to detect an eavesdropper.

prerequisites.tech: Dedicated dark fibre or free-space links
prerequisites.why: QKD needs low-loss, low-noise paths; sharing fibre with strong classical traffic degrades it.
the public discussion between the two ends must itself be unforgeable or the protocol is defeated.
losses limit fibre links to roughly a few hundred kilometres; repeaters would remove that limit.
interoperability between vendors and formal security evaluation are still maturing.

prerequisites.tech: Quantum computers running Shor's algorithm at scale
prerequisites.why: this is the threat that motivates the whole field — harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks on today's public-key encryption.

pathway.milestone: metro QKD links and short backbones in operation, plus entanglement links between cities and to satellites
pathway.unlocks: proof that quantum key distribution works outside the laboratory.

pathway.milestone: chip-scale QKD modules and national trusted-node networks alongside NIST's post-quantum cryptography standards
pathway.unlocks: cheaper, standardised deployment — with post-quantum software protecting most traffic first, since it needs no new hardware.

pathway.milestone: entanglement-based satellite links and intercontinental key exchange
pathway.unlocks: key distribution between continents without trusting every intermediate node.

pathway.milestone: quantum repeaters and early quantum networks connecting processors as well as keys
pathway.unlocks: genuinely long-distance quantum communication, and eventually a quantum internet.
